title: The Column: The Breakout from Srebrenica
sources: ICTY Krstic Trial Judgement (IT-98-33-T), paras 546, 598 (the column; genocide finding)
ICTY Popovic et al. Trial Judgement (IT-05-88-T)
ICJ Bosnia v. Serbia (2007), genocide finding
source_note: The listed adjudicative and institutional sources bound the chronology, actors, and findings described. The essay is original synthesis and does not extend individual liability, command responsibility, or institutional findings beyond the cited record.
content:
When Srebrenica fell on the evening of 11 July 1995, thousands of Bosniak men — soldiers of the ARBiH 28th Division and military-age civilians who feared capture — did not go to the United Nations compound at Potočari. Instead they gathered near the villages of Šušnjari and Jaglići on the enclave's northwestern edge and set out on foot, in a single vast column, to reach Bosnian-government territory near Tuzla across roughly a hundred kilometres of Serb-held ground.

The International Criminal Tribunal found the column to have numbered between ten and fifteen thousand men, around a third of them soldiers. It moved under near-constant attack — shelled, ambushed at defiles along its route, and at points induced or compelled to surrender under promises of safety that were not kept. Many who surrendered were executed and buried in mass graves, findings later established in detail before the Tribunal. Of those who set out, the Tribunal found that between eight and ten thousand were eventually reported as missing.

Only a portion broke through. After days of fighting a corridor opened to Bosnian-held territory near Tuzla, and the survivors crossed into the lines of the ARBiH 2nd Corps. The old formations of the enclave had, in effect, ceased to exist as coherent units; the remnant that reached Tuzla was in time reformed under the same divisional name.

The killing of the Bosnian Muslim men of Srebrenica — at Potočari and along the column together — was found by the Tribunal in Prosecutor v. Krstić to constitute genocide, the first such finding in its history, affirmed on appeal and echoed in the judgments that followed. It is remembered in Bosnia as the Marš smrti — the March of Death.
